sn22.59:1.1: This is the famous “second discourse”, the story of which is told in the Vinaya ([pli-tv-kd1:6.32.1]()). At the conclusion of the Dhammacakkappavattanasutta ([sn56.11]()), when Koṇḍañña became a stream-enterer, the Buddha continued to teach the five ascetics over several days, until all five had realized stream-entry and gone forth officially as Buddhist mendicants. Knowing they were ready, he then taught them about not-self.
sn22.59:2.2: This conditional argument against the “self” is found only here in this form, although the same manner of argument is also at [mn35:13.4](). See too the Buddha’s discussion with Poṭṭhapāda on various kinds of “self” ([dn9:21.4]()).
sn22.59:2.3: This responds to the “inner controller” (_antaryāmin_) of Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7. Uddālaka, having learned this from the centaur Kabandha in Madra (near modern Islamabad), challenges Yājñavalkya, who explains it as the self who lives in the midst of all things, unknown but knowing, controlling all from within.
sn22.59:6.1: While first argument is not stock, the remainder of the discourse is repeated countless times throughout the discourses. The Buddha engages his audience in a question and answer dialogue, stimulating reflection and giving encouragement.
sn22.59:6.8: To the five mendicants, the “self” is a metaphysical theory that there is an abiding, eternal reality that is one’s truest essence, from which we have become alienated due to defiling influences. Salvation from the travails of the world lies in realizing this essential truth. This has only a contingent relationship with the psychological “self” which grows and changes. It follows that what is impermanent cannot be the self, because when it disappears the self would also disappear ([dn15:29.4]()). And what is suffering cannot be the self, because our true essence is free of impurities and thus essentially blissful, radiant, and all-knowing. This salvific self cannot be identified with something that brings only pain ([sn22.60:5.1]()).
